Name: The Oppian Sumptuary Law and the Protest of Roman Matrons
RagShortTexts: In 215 BC the tribune Oppius passed a wartime sumptuary law restricting women's gold and purple garments
Women were forbidden to own more than half an ounce of gold or to wear richly dyed clothing
Roman women took to the streets and surrounded the Forum demanding repeal, sparking a fierce constitutional debate
BaseText: In 215 BC, the year after the Battle of Cannae, the Roman treasury was empty and its gold exhausted. The plebeian tribune Gaius Oppius passed a severe wartime sumptuary law, the Lex Oppia. It strictly forbade any Roman woman to own more than half an ounce of gold, to wear conspicuous purple or striped embroidered clothes, or to ride in a two-wheeled carriage within one mile of the city. The women of the whole city donated all their gold and silver jewelry to fund the soldiers' pay. But as Rome gradually gained the upper hand in the later years of the war, the women could not bear for the wartime ban to become a permanent shackle. Thousands of Roman matrons took to the streets, surrounded the entrances of the Senate and the Forum, and publicly petitioned and protested to the consuls and tribunes, setting off the first open political storm over women's civil rights in Roman history.

Variants.Content: The soldiers at the front are bleeding in the mud. How can the women and children at home indulge in the vanity of gold and murex-purple robes? Simplicity and restraint are the foundation of victory over Carthage!

We gave our sons, our husbands and the gold jewelry of our dowries. Now that the dawn of peace has appeared, why must the shackles of wartime still strip Roman matrons of the honor and dignity they are due?
The Romans even have to snatch women's hairpins and earrings to keep the war going. Such desperate straits only show that their empire is an empty shell, strong outside and hollow within.
